INTRO_TITLE: Use Case: New Content & Original Series
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a producer or a publisher uses Oddtoe for new content, from a premise on a page to a pilot in front of a commissioner. The worked example is an original animated series, satire with a point of view, pitched with characters, a bible and a generative-AI pilot. The same steps apply to a documentary sequence, a weekly gag strip, or a character a channel wants to own.
INTRO_COL2: Come to Oddtoe for stories with an author attached. I write and draw my own series: The Oddtoe TV Show, a satirical newscast that openly cuts corners, and Wire Taps, an animated comedy built from secretly recorded conversations. Both were written and animated in the studio, and there is a series bible and a pilot animation to show. Before that came political cartoons for a Washington DC paper, and a gag cartoon drawn every week since 2021. A producer buys an idea, and an idea is easier to buy when the person who had it can also write the script, draw the cast and make the pilot.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe can handle the first three stages of a series — where the joke starts, how the world gets written down in a bible, and how a script turns into an animatic that a commissioner can actually sit and watch.
DRAW1_BODY: The stage I would do for nothing. What is the premise, and what is the joke that gets told again every episode? A newscast that cuts corners. A soap opera made from everyone’s phone calls. The point of view comes first. A format without one is a format anyone could have pitched.
DRAW2_BODY: Everything gets written down flat before anything moves: who the characters are, what they want, what the rules of the world are, and what a typical episode looks like. Here, a diagram of how one character’s voice turns into pictures. A commissioner reads the bible in ten minutes and knows whether there is a season in it.
DRAW3_BODY: The script read against rough drawings, and timed. Here a joke that worked on the page turns out to need two more seconds, or none at all. The animatic is the cheapest version of the show that can still be watched, and I would sooner show a producer that than a deck. Get the timing right here and the pilot is mostly finishing.

PANEL_TITLE: What a Pilot Does in the Room
PANEL_INTRO: A concept clip: a caricature balloon at a field rally, animated in the studio to see whether the idea held up. It is a minute of something moving, and that gets watched. So what does a pilot do for a producer? It shortens the meeting. Commissioners watch a minute of it and know, where a deck leaves them guessing. What you count afterwards:
PANEL_ITEM1_TEXT: Commissioners and platforms who watched the pilot and asked for the bible
PANEL_ITEM2_TEXT: Whether the pilot turned into a development deal, an option, or a series order
PANEL_ITEM3_TEXT: If it goes to a channel first: views, how much of it people watched, and subscribers against the month before
PANEL_OUTRO: I like a pilot to have somewhere to go before it is finished: a pitch, a platform, or a channel of your own. Oddtoe shares a founder with the Datalabs Agency, a data visualisation studio, so if the series goes straight to a channel, a dashboard of how it is doing can be part of the job.

CIRCLE1_TITLE: The Series With An Author Attached
CIRCLE1_BODY: Satire or comedy with a point of view, written and drawn by one person, and pitched with characters, a bible and a pilot. The Oddtoe TV Show is one: a nightly newscast that openly cuts corners, written as a first series of eight episodes at eleven minutes each.
CIRCLE2_TITLE: The Pilot You Can Afford To Lose
CIRCLE2_BODY: A short made with generative-AI animation, so a producer can test an idea at a cost they could risk twice. If it lands, it is the pilot. If it does not, it is a small line on the development budget and a lesson about the premise.
CIRCLE3_BODY: A documentary has a hole where the footage should be: the meeting, the crime, the year before the camera arrived. Animated sequences drawn in the film’s own style fill it, with maps, timelines and clippings that move, from someone who designed interactive work for National Geographic Kids.
CIRCLE4_BODY: A single-panel gag cartoon, square, drawn every week since 2021 by a former political cartoonist, and available to a newspaper, a magazine or a platform through syndication. One joke, one picture, a reader gets it in a second, and your name sits above it.
CIRCLE5_BODY: A character designed for a channel, a franchise or a game: drawn once, then walking, talking, printed on a lunchbox and worn as a costume. You own the drawings, as agreed up front, so nobody has to ask before the next use.
CIRCLE6_TITLE: The Stunt, Shot As An Episode
CIRCLE6_BODY: The object from the publicity stunt page, a monument-scale head in a street, filmed as content: one episode of a series, with the build and the reaction as the story. The stunt gets a second life on a channel, and the channel gets a day nobody could have staged in a studio.
WHO_COL1: Independent producers building a slate, development executives at broadcasters and streamers, publishers of comics and strips, documentary producers, and channels that want a character of their own. What they have in common is a commissioner to convince and nothing yet to show them. Producers want ideas with an author attached, because a format is easier to sell when one person can write it, draw it and make the pilot. Documentary producers have a hole in the edit where no footage exists, and a deadline for filling it.
WHO_COL2: Publishers want a strip or a gag series that turns up every week without a writers’ room, and a character that readers recognise on the page and on a phone. Channels and brands want a character they own outright, designed once and used on a series, a game and a costume. Oddtoe has drawn cartoons and designed games and interactive work for National Geographic Kids. Agencies pitching on behalf of any of the above are welcome too: see generative-AI animation for how the pilot gets made.
TIMELINE_TITLE: A SERIES, FROM PREMISE TO PITCH
TIMELINE_ARIA: Stages of an original animated series
STEP1_TITLE: Every slate needs one thing with a name on it
STEP1_BODY: A slate fills up with formats that anyone could have pitched, and a commissioner has seen every one of them twice this week. What gets a meeting is a premise with a point of view and a person behind it. So before anything is drawn we settle one question: what is this show about, and why is it still funny in episode eight?
STEP1_CRAFT: Editorial judgement, from years of cartooning to a deadline
STEP1_CAPTION: Notes on the page before anything is drawn
STEP2_BODY: Character sheets first, because that is where the show lives: who they are, how they stand, what they want and what they never get. Then the bible: the rules of the world, a typical episode, and a season of loglines. In this example it is a newscast that cuts corners and says so on air. You approve the cast on paper before anyone records a line.
STEP2_CRAFT: Character design, drawn flat before anything moves
STEP2_CAPTION: Drawings pinned above the bench, with a maquette to check them against
STEP3_BODY: The pilot script gets read aloud against rough drawings and cut to time. A joke that worked on the page turns out to need a pause, or a cut, or to go. This is the cheapest version of the show that can still be watched, and it is the version where the format gets fixed. You see it before a single frame is animated.
STEP3_CAPTION: A frame from the animatic, where the voice turns red
STEP4_TITLE: Animated at a cost you can risk
STEP4_BODY: The pilot is animated here in the studio with generative-AI animation, guided by the drawings you approved, with voice and sound. It costs what a producer can risk on a test, so it can be made before anyone has said yes. That changes what you walk into a meeting with. A commissioner does not have to imagine the show.
STEP4_CAPTION: Projection run live from a laptop
STEP5_TITLE: A bible, a pilot, and somewhere to send them
STEP5_BODY: The pilot goes wherever the idea has a chance: a pitch to a broadcaster or a streamer, a platform that commissions shorts, or a channel of your own where the audience decides. The package is the same each time: the bible, the character sheets, the pilot, and a season of loglines. Oddtoe comes to the pitch if you want the author in the room.
STEP5_CRAFT: The pitch, with the author in the room
STEP5_CAPTION: The show, lit, on a stage
STEP6_TITLE: A format that does not go back in the drawer
STEP6_BODY: Whatever the commissioner says, you own what was made: the format, the characters, the bible and the pilot, with rights set out in writing before the pilot starts. A no from one broadcaster leaves you with a finished pitch for the next one. A yes leaves you with a first series already designed.
STEP6_CAPTION: Made once. Still there years later
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_COL1: I make my own series when nobody has asked for one. The Oddtoe TV Show and Wire Taps both started as jokes I wanted to see made, and the gag cartoon has gone out every week since 2021 with no editor asking for it. That is most of why this brief grabs me. A producer looking for new content is asking for the thing I would be making anyway, with a commissioner waiting at the end of it instead of a drawer.
WHY_COL2: The other reason is generative-AI animation. For a long time the pilot was the expensive part, so ideas died in decks. Now the pilot can be made in the studio at a cost a producer can risk, by a comedy writer who also draws, without a crew. The practical upside for a producer is that the person pitching the format has a stake in whether it gets made. I want the commissioner to laugh for the same reason you do.

WYG_TITLE: What Does a Producer Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: A format with an author attached: the bible, the character artwork, a pilot script and a finished pilot. All of it is yours to pitch, with rights set out in writing before the pilot starts. • The bible — premise, world, characters and a season of loglines • Character sheets — the cast drawn flat, for the pitch and for the animators • The pilot script and the animatic it was timed against • The pilot — made with generative-AI animation, with voice and sound • Rights as agreed, in writing
WYG_COL2: People tend to forget about the artwork. Because the pilot is built from finished character designs, the producer also owns drawings that work on a poster, a thumbnail, a sticker and a costume without redrawing anything. It can be whatever the slate needs: an original animated series, a documentary sequence, a weekly gag strip, a character for a channel, or a stunt filmed as an episode. They are written and drawn in the same studio, so what goes on screen is the same character as the one on the page.
PKG1_BODY: We work out the premise and the joke before we work out the format. Bring the gap on the slate, a deadline, and whatever you already have, even if it is one line.
PKG2_KICKER: Drawn until you can see it
PKG2_BODY: Character sheets, the bible, and the animatic. You sign off on the cast and a timed script before anything is animated.
PKG3_BODY: What a pilot costs to risk and how long it takes. Voice, sound and music rights. And the pitch date, which nobody can move.
PKG4_BODY: Written and animated in Melbourne with generative-AI animation, voice and sound, from the drawings you approved. Finished so it plays in a meeting, on a phone, and on a channel.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports, a delivery schedule against your pitch date, and one person to ring about all of it.
CRED_COL1: A gag cartoon and an animated series are the same job at different lengths. One picture and one line have to be funny with no explanation, and if you need a second panel you have already lost the reader. Oddtoe drew editorial cartoons at college in Delaware, then worked as political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper. Years of finding the one joke a story would carry, and watching an editor bin the ones that needed a caption.
CRED_COL2: Since then, a stage and two series. A 2.1-metre baobab with live projection for Babbling with Baobabs, a kids’ comedy show at the Melbourne Comedy Festival in 2019. Then two original series, written and animated in the studio, and the weekly gag cartoon. The same instinct decides what a series should be. Commissioners read a hundred loglines and remember one. It also decides what to leave out: a premise that needs a paragraph has failed.

FAQ.q: What does this new content use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of new content for a producer or a publisher. It follows one brief - a slate with a gap and nothing to show a commissioner - from the premise through characters and a bible, a timed script, a pilot made with generative-AI animation, and the pitch, to what the producer still owns afterwards. It uses an original animated series as the example, and a documentary sequence, a weekly gag strip, or a character for a channel would follow the same shape.

FAQ.q: How long does an animated pilot take?
FAQ.a: [Oddtoe: fill] from premise to a finished pilot. The premise and the bible come first, the animatic next, and the pilot is animated once the timed script is signed off. A rush is possible, and it comes out of the writing stage, which is the part worth protecting.

FAQ.q: What does an original animated series cost?
FAQ.a: Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by how many episodes, how long each one is, how many characters, and whether the job stops at the pilot or runs to a first series. It is costed the same way as every other job at the studio, from a pilot to prop fabrication. Send the premise and the pitch date and you get a quote.

FAQ.q: Can an original animated series be pitched outside Australia?
FAQ.a: Yes. A pilot and a bible travel as files, and nothing has to be shipped. Oddtoe has business contacts in Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for a pitch in Europe or the United States. Voice can be recorded in whatever accent the market needs.

FAQ.q: Who owns the characters and the format of the series afterwards?
FAQ.a: That is settled in writing before the pilot starts, and it can be set up either way: rights assigned to the producer or publisher, or shared with the author. Whatever is agreed, you keep the bible, the character artwork and the pilot, so a no from one commissioner is a finished pitch for the next.

FAQ.q: Can the pilot be reused if the series is commissioned?
FAQ.a: Usually, yes. The pilot is made from the same character drawings and the same timed script as the series, so it can run as episode one, or be remade with what the pitch taught you. Either way the bible and the character artwork carry straight into the first series without redrawing anything.

FAQ.q: Is the pilot made with generative AI, and do you do the animation as well?
FAQ.a: Yes to both. The writing and the animation happen in the same studio, and the pilot is made with generative-AI animation guided by the character drawings you approved, with voice and sound. See what generative AI animation is and the animation studio.
Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.
